outcome: Not settled as stated. Since 26 January 2024 the Hamiltonian-path question for connected vertex-transitive graphs remains open in every source read; progress is on restricted classes (odd order by a 2024 unrefereed preprint; Cayley graphs of degree above n¹⁻ᶜ by a 2026 preprint; orders 6p, 10p, 2pq and some families by Hamilton-cycle results) and on longest-cycle bounds, which reached a linear bound on 1 October 2026 with the authors crediting ChatGPT (GPT-6) with the route to the main criterion.
problem_asks: (1) For every finite connected vertex-transitive graph G, G contains a Hamiltonian path (a path through every vertex exactly once). That is the whole claim: universal over all orders, with no exceptional graphs listed. Scope note: the bullet says ‘symmetric graphs’. The Wikipedia lead (encyclopedia, 12 March 2025 edit) and the Open Problem Garden both state the class as vertex-transitive, and that reading is used here. If ‘symmetric’ were read as arc-transitive, the asked class is a proper subclass and every result below on vertex-transitive graphs would cover it only a fortiori. Not asked by the statement: Hamiltonian cycles (Thomassen’s variant, which has five known exceptions), longest-path or longest-cycle lengths, Babai’s contrary conjecture; these are neighbouring questions and are recorded as such where they appear.

events.what_happened: Misa Nakanishi (sole author), arXiv preprint ‘Proof of Lovász conjecture for odd order’ (arXiv:2407.00646). Claims every connected vertex-transitive graph with an odd number of vertices is Hamiltonian (Theorem 3.1), which gives a Hamiltonian path for odd orders. The abstract says Lovász conjectured the path statement in 1970.
events.revisions: v1 30 Jun 2024 (arXiv listing reports 43 KB); v2 10 Jul 2024 (3 KB); v3 30 Jul 2024 (3 KB, current). The size change between v1 and v2 is reported by the listing; I did not determine why.
events.delivers: Every connected vertex-transitive graph of odd order is Hamiltonian, so has a Hamiltonian path. Restricted to odd order. Its argument does not reach even orders, where the known non-Hamiltonian examples (Petersen, Coxeter and their truncations) all lie.
events.remains: All connected vertex-transitive graphs of even order. The odd-order case is the only part the event addresses.
events.directly_checkable: Not a finite object. The argument is a recursion: Lemma 3.1 gives a 2-factor of an odd number of equal odd cycles, and Theorem 3.1 contracts the cycles and recurses, lifting a Hamiltonian cycle back. A reader can check it by hand; I did not complete that check.
events.doubts: Read via the fetch tool’s summaries of the v1 and v3 HTML, so the wording below is as returned and not byte-verified. (a) Lemma 3.1 asserts ‘Since |G| is odd, ℛ(A) ≠ ∅ and |ℛ(A)| is odd’ with no justification in the text as read. (b) Theorem 3.1 says ‘Now, H₂ has a hamilton cycle’ and proceeds by recursion; no argument is shown that the contraction terminates, and the lifting step is only sketched (‘By reversing these operations…’). (c) Lemma 3.1 calls the complete and 2-regular cases ‘obvious’, and case (b) says ‘we can easily take i odd cycles with the same length’. (d) No journal publication, erratum, referee report or public comment was found. The 2025–2026 papers whose reference lists I read do not cite it: Bedert et al. (2603.08675), Bucić et al. (2606.09742), Zhou (2608.02349), Li–Methuku (2609.38135), Ma–Zhao (2610.02053). The reference list of Chen–Li–Yu (2506.19888) could not be read. Those later papers describe the conjecture as open and do not mention odd order. Silence alone is not a reason to doubt; it is recorded because a claim to settle all odd orders of a 1970 problem has no visible uptake.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture for odd orders: asserts the Hamiltonian (cycle) property, which implies the path claim there.
people: Misa Nakanishi (sole author; no institution stated on the page; the email domain suggests Keio University, not confirmed)

events.what_happened: Carla Groenland, Sean Longbrake, Raphael Steiner, Jérémie Turcotte, Liana Yepremyan, ‘Longest cycles in vertex-transitive and highly connected graphs’ (arXiv:2408.04618). Shows every connected vertex-transitive graph on n ≥ 3 vertices has a cycle, and so a path, of length Ω(n¹³⁄²¹), improving DeVos’s (1−o(1))n³⁄⁵. Also bounds intersections of longest cycles in highly connected graphs.
events.delivers: A longest cycle, and hence a longest path, of length Ω(n¹³⁄²¹) in every connected vertex-transitive graph on n ≥ 3 vertices. A length bound only.
events.remains: Whether a path through all n vertices exists. A path of length n¹³⁄²¹ does not settle that.

checked_by.who: Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published as Bull. Lond. Math. Soc. 57 (2025), no. 10, 2975–2990, according to the bibliography of Ma–Zhao (arXiv:2610.02053). I did not open the journal page.

events.direction: Partial and toward the conjecture only in the weak sense of long paths. Does not claim Hamiltonicity.

events.what_happened: Sergey Norin, Raphael Steiner, Stéphan Thomassé, Paul Wollan, ‘Small hitting sets for longest paths and cycles’ (arXiv:2505.08634). Corollary 2: every connected vertex-transitive graph on n ≥ 3 vertices contains a cycle, and a path, of length Ω(n⁹⁄¹⁴). Main tools: lpt(G) ≤ √(8n) for connected graphs, and lpt(G) ≤ O(ℓ⁵⁄⁹).
events.delivers: A longest path and cycle of length Ω(n⁹⁄¹⁴) in connected vertex-transitive graphs. A length bound only.
events.remains: Whether a Hamiltonian path exists.

checked_by.who: Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published as Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 154 (2026), no. 6, 2319–2335, per the bibliography of Ma–Zhao (arXiv:2610.02053). Journal page not opened.

events.direction: Partial and toward the conjecture only through a path-length bound. No Hamiltonicity claim.

events.what_happened: Shaofei Du and Tianlei Zhou, ‘Hamilton cycles in vertex-transitive graphs of order 6p’ (arXiv:2409.06138). Every connected vertex-transitive graph of order 6p (p prime) has a Hamiltonian cycle except the triangle-replaced Petersen graph, which is the truncation of the Petersen graph (order 30). The Hamiltonian path for all such graphs was already known from Kutnar and Šparl (see kutnar-sparl-2007-order-6p).
events.delivers: Hamiltonian cycles, hence paths, for connected vertex-transitive graphs of order 6p (p prime), except the truncated Petersen graph. For the path question the 6p case was already settled by Kutnar and Šparl; this event strengthens the cycle form on that class.
events.remains: All other orders.
events.direction: Toward the cycle version on order 6p; the path claim on that class was already known.

events.what_happened: Shaofei Du, Wenjuan Luo, Hao Yu, ‘On Hamilton paths in vertex-transitive graphs of order 10p’ (arXiv:2411.17780). Treats the exceptional family left open by Kutnar, Marušič and Zhang (2012): connected graphs admitting a vertex-transitive PSL(2, s^m) action with a point stabiliser of the stated form, where s is prime and s^m+1 = 2p. Shows these have Hamiltonian cycles, and so Hamiltonian paths.
events.revisions: v1 26 Nov 2024 (submitted by Hao Yu); no later version found in the listing read.
events.delivers: Hamiltonian cycles, hence paths, for the exceptional family of connected vertex-transitive graphs of order 10p (p prime, p ≠ 7) identified by Kutnar, Marušič and Zhang. Together with the 2012 result, this gives Hamiltonian paths for order 10p with p ≠ 7 (as I read the hypotheses).
events.remains: Order 10p with p = 7 (excluded by the hypothesis as read) and all other orders.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture on a restricted class (order 10p, one family). Hamilton-cycle form.

events.what_happened: Huye Chen, Jingjian Li, Hao Yu, ‘Hamilton cycles in vertex-transitive graphs of order 10p’ (arXiv:2506.19888). Every connected vertex-transitive graph of order 10p (p prime) has a Hamiltonian cycle except the truncation of the Petersen graph.
events.delivers: Hamiltonian cycles, hence paths, for connected vertex-transitive graphs of order 10p (p prime) except the truncated Petersen graph (order 30). The truncated Petersen graph is one of the cycle exceptions; its path status is not stated in the text I could read.
events.remains: All other orders.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture on order 10p; Hamilton-cycle form with one exception.

events.what_happened: Benjamin Bedert, Nemanja Draganić, Alp Müyesser, Matías Pavez-Signé, ‘The Lovász conjecture holds for moderately dense Cayley graphs’ (arXiv:2603.08675). Proves an absolute c ≥ 1/200 such that, for large n, every connected n-vertex Cayley graph of degree d > n¹⁻ᶜ has a Hamiltonian cycle. Method: an arithmetic regularity lemma specialised to Cayley graphs, in place of Szemerédi’s regularity lemma. The paper says the dense case (degree εn) is due to Christofides, Hladký and Máthé.
events.revisions: v1 9 Mar 2026; v2 20 Apr 2026 (current; the listing says ‘some corrections and simplifications’, without detail).
events.delivers: Hamiltonian cycles, hence paths, for Cayley graphs of degree above n¹⁻ᶜ, for large n. Restricted to Cayley graphs and to degrees above n¹⁻ᶜ; the authors say their methods cannot go much beyond degree n¹⁄² and leave degree n^(o(1)) open.
events.remains: Non-Cayley connected vertex-transitive graphs; Cayley graphs of degree at most n¹⁻ᶜ, including the n^(o(1)) range the authors leave open; the small-n range.

checked_by.qualification: Active researchers in extremal and probabilistic graph theory; affiliations not read
checked_by.what_they_did: Built on the result: their robust percolation theorem for Cayley graphs (Theorem 1.9) is said to recover the Bedert et al. Hamiltonicity result at percolation parameter p = 1, with a worse constant; they credit Bedert et al. for Theorem 1.8. This is use of the result, not a referee report.

events.direction: Toward the conjecture on a restricted class, in the conjectured direction (Hamiltonicity). Title frames it as the conjecture holding for that class.

events.what_happened: Domagoj Bradač and Oliver Janzer, ‘Hamiltonicity of regular sublinear expanders’ (arXiv:2605.15043). Proves an absolute K such that any n-vertex d-regular γ-expander with d ≥ (γ⁻¹ log n)^K is Hamiltonian, if the graph is bipartite or γ-far from bipartite. Also a percolation version for Cayley graphs (Theorem 1.9), applied to Cayley and Kneser graphs.
events.delivers: Hamiltonian cycles in regular expanders whose degree is at least polylogarithmic in n (with K absolute), bipartite or far from bipartite. For Cayley graphs, the percolated-graph result with degree and percolation constraints. Whether this covers all Cayley graphs of degree n^(o(1)) is not established by me.
events.remains: Non-expander Cayley graphs; regular graphs that are not expanders; non-Cayley vertex-transitive graphs in general.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture on a restricted class (polylog-degree expanders, Cayley graphs with the stated percolation condition). Hamiltonicity direction.

events.what_happened: Matija Bucić, Micha Christoph, Alexey Pokrovskiy, Raphael Steiner, ‘Towards the Lovász conjecture via sublinear expanders’ (arXiv:2606.09742). Proves every connected vertex-transitive graph of order n has a cycle of length at least n^(2/3−ε) for every ε > 0 and sufficiently large n (Theorem 1.1), improving Norin et al.’s n^(9/14). The authors say the approach meets a natural barrier for several existing methods. The bibliography cites a companion ‘Lovász conjecture holds asymptotically’ working draft (2026, ‘in preparation’) that I could not locate.
events.delivers: A longest-cycle bound of order n^(2/3−o(1)) in connected vertex-transitive graphs. A length bound only.
events.remains: Whether a Hamiltonian path exists.
events.direction: Partial and toward the conjecture only through a longest-cycle bound.

events.what_happened: Bowen Li and Abhishek Methuku, ‘Long Directed Cycles in Vertex-Transitive Digraphs’ (arXiv:2607.05807). Results on directed cycles in connected vertex-transitive digraphs: a construction with perimeter gap at least (1−o(1))·ln n for infinitely many n, and a directed cycle of length Ω(√n) in every such digraph (Theorem 1.5 as read). The undirected Lovász statement appears only as background.
events.delivers: Results on directed cycles in vertex-transitive digraphs. Discounted for this problem: the bullet concerns undirected graphs and Hamiltonian paths, and these results do not address either.
events.remains: Everything in the undirected problem.
events.direction: Neither toward nor against the bullet; a neighbouring directed-graph result.

events.what_happened: Bowen Li and Abhishek Methuku, ‘A nearly linear bound for the Lovász conjecture’ (arXiv:2609.38135, 21 pages). Proves every connected vertex-transitive graph on n vertices contains a cycle of length n¹⁻ᵒ⁽¹⁾, improving the n²⁄³⁻ᵒ⁽¹⁾ bound of Bucić, Christoph, Pokrovskiy and Steiner. The proof uses a structure theorem of Tessera and Tointon, the Lovász local lemma, and Babai’s contraction lemma.
events.delivers: A cycle of length n¹⁻ᵒ⁽¹⁾ in every connected vertex-transitive graph on n vertices. Not Hamiltonian and not a path through all vertices. Its title frames the result as a bound for the Lovász conjecture.
events.remains: Hamiltonian path existence; the gap between n¹⁻ᵒ⁽¹⁾ and n.
events.direction: Partial and toward the conjecture only through a cycle-length bound.

systems.name: GPT-5.6 Sol
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors’ ‘Statement of AI use’: in July 2026 they asked OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol whether a decomposition into vertex-transitive parts was possible, and it directed them to the Tessera–Tointon structure theorem, which the authors say supplied the partition for the single-orbit and large-orbit cases. For the small-orbit case the model pointed them to Babai’s contraction lemma and supplied the group-theoretic arguments for controlling the number and word lengths of the generators, keeping the loss to m^(o(1)). The authors say AI was used to polish and rewrite the manuscript and that they take full responsibility for the content. The authors do not say whether the model originated any step of the cycle argument beyond these.
systems.basis_quote: In July 2026, when the authors asked OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol whether a decomposition into vertex-transitive parts is possible, it directed them to the structure theorem of Tessera and Tointon [35]. GPT pointed them to Babai's contraction lemma. GPT supplied the required group-theoretic arguments for controlling both the number and the word lengths of the required generators. The authors also used AI assistance to polish and rewrite parts of this manuscript and take full responsibility for the final content.

events.what_happened: Jie Ma and Ziyuan Zhao, ‘Linear circumference in vertex-transitive graphs’ (arXiv:2610.02053). Proves an absolute c > 0 such that every connected vertex-transitive graph on n ≥ 3 vertices has a cycle of length at least cn; for degree d at least some d₀, a cycle of length at least (1 − d⁻¹⁄¹⁰⁰)n. The authors call it ‘the first linear bound toward Lovász’s Hamiltonicity conjecture’. Method: a general criterion (Theorem 1.2) on separations of the graph, built from DFS families of disjoint cycles merged by Mader’s packing theorem; for vertex-transitive graphs, a ball-growth lemma (Lemma 3.1), or otherwise the DeVos–Mohar structure theorem.
events.delivers: A cycle of length linear in n in every connected vertex-transitive graph on n ≥ 3 vertices (and (1 − d⁻¹⁄¹⁰⁰)n for large degree). Not Hamiltonian and not a path through all vertices.
events.remains: Hamiltonian path existence; the step from a linear cycle to a spanning path.
events.direction: Partial and toward the conjecture only through a cycle-length bound. It is the strongest circumference bound I found; Li–Methuku’s n¹⁻ᵒ⁽¹⁾ is weaker.
people: Jie Ma (USTC, Hefei; Yau Mathematical Sciences Center, Tsinghua)

systems.name: ChatGPT (GPT-6)
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors’ AI-use declaration: used to assist with the exploration of proof strategies, the formulation and testing of intermediate claims, and the preparation of the manuscript. The authors say the GPT-6 exchanges (the sentence naming them was not retrieved verbatim) led to the general criterion of Theorem 1.2, which draws on Tessera–Tointon, Segal–Verstraëte and Mader’s theorem. They say they directed the process, independently checked the proofs and take full responsibility. Exploration resumed with GPT-6 in September 2026, and earlier GPT-5-series attempts did not yield improvements toward the conjecture.
systems.basis_quote: ChatGPT (GPT-6) was used to assist with the exploration of proof strategies, the formulation and testing of intermediate claims, and the preparation of this manuscript. These tools eventually led to Theorem 1.2, giving a general criterion for finding long cycles. The authors directed this process, independently checked the proofs, and take full responsibility for the mathematical content and presentation.

events.what_happened: Tianlei Zhou (Zhou Tianlei in the abstract metadata), ‘On Hamilton cycles in connected vertex-transitive graphs of order 2pq’ (arXiv:2608.02349). Proves every connected non-quasiprimitive vertex-transitive graph of order 2pq (p, q distinct primes) that has a maximal intransitive normal subgroup inducing prime-length orbits contains a Hamiltonian cycle. The abstract says all connected vertex-transitive graphs of order pq are Hamiltonian except the Petersen graph, and that primitive graphs of order 2pq are resolved except the Coxeter graph.
events.delivers: Hamiltonian cycles, hence paths, for the non-quasiprimitive connected vertex-transitive graphs of order 2pq with the stated intransitive-normal-subgroup hypothesis. Restricted to order 2pq and that structural class.
events.remains: Other orders and the other structural cases, including primitive graphs beyond the cases cited in the abstract.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture on a restricted class (order 2pq, one structural case). Hamilton-cycle form.

events.what_happened: Matija Bucić, Kevin Hendrey, Bojan Mohar, Raphael Steiner, Liana Yepremyan, ‘Long cycles in vertex transitive digraphs’ (arXiv:2602.16333). Shows every connected vertex-transitive digraph on n ≥ 2 vertices has a directed cycle of length Ω(n¹⁄³); constructs such digraphs with perimeter gap at least (1−o(1))·ln n, answering Alspach’s 1981 question. Also gives a path-versus-cycle argument that re-proves Babai’s undirected result.
events.delivers: Directed-cycle length results for vertex-transitive digraphs. Discounted for this problem: the main results concern directed cycles; the undirected Hamiltonicity conjectures appear as motivation.
events.remains: Everything in the undirected Hamiltonian-path problem.
events.direction: Neither toward nor against the bullet; neighbouring directed-graph result.

events.what_happened: Jie Ma and Ziyuan Zhao, ‘Intersections of longest cycles in vertex-transitive and highly connected graphs’ (arXiv:2508.17438). Shows any two longest cycles in a connected vertex-transitive graph on n vertices share at least f(n) vertices, with f(n) → ∞, resolving a question of Babai (1979) for this class; also improves a bound of Groenland et al. for highly connected graphs.
events.delivers: A lower bound on the intersection of longest cycles in vertex-transitive graphs. Discounted for this problem: it concerns the overlap of longest cycles, not a Hamiltonian path.
events.remains: Everything in the Hamiltonian-path problem.
events.direction: Neither toward nor against the bullet; a neighbouring cycle-intersection result.

events.what_happened: GitHub pull request #5193 in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, ‘Add Lovász’s conjecture (Hamiltonian paths in vertex-transitive graphs)’, by henrykmichalewski, opened 28 Aug 2026. Adds FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/LovaszConjecture.lean, stating that every finite connected vertex-transitive graph has a Hamiltonian path (Mathlib Walk.IsHamiltonian), with variants (Babai’s long-cycle bound; the dense case of Christofides–Hladký–Máthé), marked sorry. The main conjecture is marked research open. At the time read the PR was open and not merged.

events.what_happened: Donald Knuth’s note ‘Claude’s Cycles’ (dated 28 Feb 2026 per secondary accounts) on splitting the arcs of a digraph on m³ vertices into three Hamiltonian cycles. Per secondary accounts only, Claude Opus 4.6 gave a construction for odd m, Knuth wrote the proof, and later work by GPT models reportedly handled even m. The Stanford PDF could not be decoded by the fetch tool, so these details are not checked against Knuth’s text.

events.delivers: A Hamiltonian-cycle decomposition of one family of Cayley digraphs (m³ vertices, three arc-disjoint Hamiltonian cycles). Discounted for this problem: it asks for a decomposition of a specific digraph, not for a Hamiltonian path in every connected vertex-transitive graph. It is recorded because it is the most visible AI-and-Hamiltonian result I found.
events.remains: Everything in this bullet.
events.directly_checkable: The construction is explicit (a rule keyed to (i+j+k) mod m in secondary accounts), but I did not verify it.
events.direction: Neither toward nor against the bullet; a neighbouring question.

events.what_happened: Torsten Mütze, ‘On Hamilton cycles in graphs defined by intersecting set systems’ (arXiv:2311.08521), an expository article. Abstract: Lovász’s conjecture ‘has recently been settled’ for graphs defined by intersecting set systems. Body: Hamiltonicity holds for all generalised Johnson graphs J(n,k,s) (vertices the k-subsets of [n], edges joining sets meeting in exactly s elements), including the Kneser graphs (s = 0) and Johnson graphs, proved by induction and relying on Kneser-graph results credited to Merino–Mütze–Namrata (2022), Mütze–Nummenpalo–Walczak (2021), Johnson (2011), Chen–Füredi (2002) and Chen (2000). The Chen–Lih (1987) formulation excludes the Petersen graph.
events.delivers: Hamilton cycles, per the article, in all generalised Johnson graphs J(n,k,s) (including Kneser and Johnson graphs), with the Petersen graph excluded. A restricted class of vertex-transitive graphs. The article is a review of earlier results and does not claim them as new; I did not read the exact exception list in the body.
events.remains: Connected vertex-transitive graphs outside the generalised Johnson family, and the Petersen exception.
events.doubts: The abstract says ‘has recently been settled’ and the body credits the Kneser results to earlier papers. I did not open those primary papers, so their scope is only as Mütze describes it.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture on a restricted class (generalised Johnson graphs, including Kneser graphs); Hamilton-cycle form with the Petersen exception.

events.remains: Connected vertex-transitive graphs outside the Kneser family.

events.what_happened: Klavdija Kutnar and Primož Šparl, ‘Hamilton paths and cycles in vertex-transitive graphs of order 6p’ (arXiv:math/0702182, submitted 7 Feb 2007). Abstract: every connected vertex-transitive graph of order 6p (p prime) has a Hamiltonian path; except for the truncation of the Petersen graph, every such graph that is not genuinely imprimitive has a Hamiltonian cycle. Published in 2009 according to Du and Zhou (2409.06138); journal not checked.

events.what_happened: Tobias Ahsendorf, ‘On a conjecture concerning vertex-transitive graphs’ (arXiv:0905.2420, submitted 14 May 2009; revised 18 May 2009). Defines a minor relation stronger than the classical one and proposes a conjecture that would imply the Lovász conjecture if true. Proves no case of the Lovász conjecture.

summary: The search found no settlement of the Lovász path conjecture for connected vertex-transitive graphs in any source read, and no claim that an AI system solved the conjecture. Searches covered the conjecture under its names and phrasings, the result words (proof, counterexample, bound), recent arXiv work on Hamiltonicity in vertex-transitive and Cayley graphs, the AI search (lab announcements, Erdős-problem and AI-math coverage, and the names of specific systems), and the Wikipedia article. The events, in order, are: restricted-class Hamiltonicity results (odd order by Nakanishi, a 2024 preprint with no visible uptake; order 6p, 10p, 2pq and pq; dense graphs; Cayley graphs of degree above n¹⁻ᶜ, a 2026 preprint built on by Bradač–Janzer; a polylog-degree expander result); longest-cycle bounds that rose from n³⁄⁵ (2023) to n¹³⁄²¹, n⁹⁄¹⁴ and n²⁄³⁻ᵒ⁽¹⁾ in 2024–2026, then to n¹⁻ᵒ⁽¹⁾ (Li–Methuku, 29 Sep 2026) and to a linear bound (Ma–Zhao, 1 Oct 2026); and discounted neighbours (directed cycles, cycle intersections, Knuth’s Hamiltonian-cycle decomposition, a Lean statement). The two most recent cycle-length papers are the only events where an AI system is credited with mathematics the result uses. Li–Methuku’s statement of AI use credits OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol with directing the authors to the Tessera–Tointon partition and supplying the group-theoretic arguments for the small-orbit case. Ma–Zhao’s declaration credits ChatGPT (GPT-6) with exploration that ‘eventually led to Theorem 1.2’, the general criterion behind a linear circumference bound. Both papers say the authors checked and take responsibility. Close calls: (a) Nakanishi’s odd-order claim is a Hamiltonian-cycle claim for a restricted class, and I could only read it through fetch summaries; its lack of any review or citation is recorded as silence, not as a verdict. (b) Whether Li–Methuku’s and Ma–Zhao’s bounds count as moving the problem at all: they bound cycle length, while the bullet asks for a spanning path; I record that they do not establish a Hamiltonian path and leave the weighing to the later pass. (c) The scope word ‘symmetric’: the bullet says ‘symmetric graphs’, but Wikipedia and the Open Problem Garden state the conjecture for vertex-transitive graphs, and I used that reading; arc-transitive would be a narrower class and would change which results apply. (d) Several sources disagree on details: the Royle–Spiga claim that the conjecture is verified by computer for all vertex-transitive graphs of order at most 100 appears only on secondary web pages and I could not confirm it, so it is not recorded as an event; a cited but unlocated working draft (Bucić–Christoph–Pokrovskiy–Steiner, ‘Lovász conjecture holds asymptotically’) is not an event I could date. The AI-attribution picture for Knuth’s Hamiltonian-cycle note comes from secondary accounts only, because its PDF did not decode, and that event is discounted as a different question.
competing_reading: Read the record as progress rather than nothing. Several events now prove the Hamiltonian-path claim (or its cycle form) for infinite restricted families: odd order (Nakanishi, if correct), Cayley graphs of degree above n¹⁻ᶜ (Bedert et al.), and orders 6p, 10p, 2pq and pq. Two September–October 2026 papers, Li–Methuku and Ma–Zhao, credit a named AI system with ideas their proofs use, and a reader could count those as AI-involved progress on the conjecture. Against that: no event settles the bullet as stated (every connected vertex-transitive graph, every order, a spanning path); the AI-credited papers bound cycle length, not path existence; the only odd-order result is unrefereed and uncited; and the restricted-class results are on classes that do not include the general case.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A referee report, journal acceptance, or Lean formalisation of Nakanishi arXiv:2407.00646, or an explicit gap in Lemma 3.1 or Theorem 3.1 that a later paper identifies. (2) The Bucić–Christoph–Pokrovskiy–Steiner working draft ‘Lovász conjecture holds asymptotically’ if it appears, to see what it covers and whether it is a claim about the path statement. (3) The exact sentence immediately before ‘These tools eventually led to Theorem 1.2’ in arXiv:2610.02053, which the fetch tool did not return verbatim, and the authors’ own account of which steps of the criterion the model originated; the same for Li–Methuku’s statement of AI use beyond the sentences quoted. (4) The bullet’s intended class: whether ‘symmetric graphs’ means vertex-transitive (as the Wikipedia lead and Open Problem Garden state) or arc-transitive. (5) For the Royle–Spiga order-100 claim, the primary paper and its scope. (6) Whether the Mütze-credited Kneser results (Merino–Mütze–Namrata 2022; Mütze–Nummenpalo–Walczak 2021) cover the stated classes, from the primary papers.

incomplete: (1) Full-text reads were done through a summarising fetch tool. The tool returned quotations in short pieces and paraphrase in places, so the quoted AI-use sentences are as returned and were cross-checked only where two separate fetches agreed (Bucić et al.; the Ma–Zhao and Li–Methuku sentences). Verify verbatim before relying on exact wording. (2) Ma–Zhao: the sentence immediately before ‘These tools eventually led to Theorem 1.2’ was not retrieved verbatim; the GPT-6 antecedent in the basis_quote is taken from a summary. (3) Chen–Li–Yu (2506.19888): the end of the HTML and the PDF did not decode, so the acknowledgements, AI-use statement and reference list (including whether Nakanishi is cited) are unread; ai.none_found is null for this reason. (4) Bradač–Janzer (2605.15043): about 59k of 159k characters were not read; the AI-use statement is unverified for that part. (5) Not read in full: Christofides–Hladký–Máthé JCTB text; DeVos 2023 full text; Ahsendorf 2009 full text; Kutnar–Šparl 2007 full text (abstract page only); Babai 1979 (original not opened); Kutnar–Marušič 2008 (not opened); Kutnar–Marušič–Zhang 2012 (not opened); Du–Kutnar–Marušič 2018 Combinatorica version (not opened). For these, ai.none_found is null where I did not read the text. (6) The Knuth ‘Claude’s Cycles’ note could not be read; its AI attribution comes from secondary accounts only, so systems is empty per the quote rule. (7) Journal publication status for Groenland et al. (Bull. LMS 2025) and Norin et al. (PAMS 2026) comes from citing bibliographies and was not checked at the journal. (8) The ‘Lovász conjecture holds asymptotically’ working draft and the Royle–Spiga order-100 check are not recorded as events because I could not locate or date a primary source. (9) Scope of the Mütze-credited Kneser results (Merino–Mütze–Namrata 2022; Mütze–Nummenpalo–Walczak 2021) is as described by Mütze; primary papers were not opened. (10) The ProofAtlas page and the Lean PR are recorded as a repository and a statement, not as results. (11) The bullet’s ‘symmetric graphs’ is read as vertex-transitive, following the Wikipedia lead and the Open Problem Garden; I did not research the arc-transitive reading separately.
